name: Dunzo
one_liner: Hyperlocal app that would pick up and deliver anything in the city, later a 15-30 minute grocery dark-store service
story: Dunzo began as a WhatsApp concierge that would fetch anything, won Google's first direct investment in India (2017) and a $240M Reliance-led round in 2022 at roughly $775M. It pivoted into 15-minute dark-store grocery delivery just as Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart out-spent it; salaries were delayed through 2023, buyout talks with Swiggy and BigBasket failed, and the app went dark in January 2025. Reliance wrote off its entire ~$200M stake (about Rs 1,645 crore) in FY25.

name: BluSmart
one_liner: All-electric ride-hailing service owning its fleet and charging superhubs
story: BluSmart ran an all-EV cab service in Delhi NCR and Bengaluru, with cars leased largely from its promoters' listed firm Gensol Engineering, and raised about $180M in equity and debt from bp ventures and others. In April 2025 SEBI found the Jaggi brothers had diverted loan money meant for EVs (Gensol bought only 4,704 of the 6,400 cars it borrowed Rs 978 crore for) into personal luxuries, barred them from markets, and BluSmart halted bookings almost overnight. Its asset-light app sat on top of a fleet it did not control, so the promoter fraud took the operator down with it.

name: GoMechanic
one_liner: Network of branded partner workshops for app-booked car servicing and repair
story: GoMechanic built a franchise network of car-service workshops and raised about $62M from Sequoia (Peak XV), Tiger Global, Orios and Chiratae, hitting a $285M valuation in 2021 and negotiating with SoftBank at up to $1B. In January 2023 the founders admitted inflating revenue; the SoftBank deal collapsed, 70% of staff were laid off and investors filed a police complaint. In March 2023 its assets went in an undisclosed slump sale to a Lifelong Group-led consortium (Servizzy), with founders left out.

name: Byju's
one_liner: K-12 and test-prep learning app with video lessons, sold on financed tablets by a large field sales force
story: Byju's became India's most valuable startup at $22B in 2022 after raising roughly $5.5B and spending billions on acquisitions (Aakash, WhiteHat Jr, Great Learning, Epic) during the pandemic edtech boom. As schools reopened demand fell, audits were delayed, it defaulted on a $1.2B US term loan and Prosus marked it to $5.1B in 2023; a 2024 rights issue was priced at about $220-250M. Lenders pushed its US unit into Chapter 11 and the parent into Indian insolvency in 2024, and the founder said it was 'worth zero'.

name: ZestMoney
one_liner: Buy-now-pay-later and checkout EMI platform for Indians without credit cards
story: Goldman Sachs- and Zip-backed ZestMoney offered BNPL and EMI credit at online checkouts and was valued at about $445-450M in 2021. A roughly $200-300M sale to PhonePe collapsed in 2023 over due diligence and bad-loan concerns, the founders resigned, and the company announced it would wind down in December 2023 after RBI tightened rules on fintech credit lines. DMI Group bought the remains in a January 2024 distress sale for an undisclosed sum.

name: Koo
one_liner: Multilingual Indian microblogging app positioned as a homegrown Twitter alternative
story: Koo surged in 2021 when Indian ministers adopted it during the government's spat with Twitter, raising $50-65M from Tiger Global, Accel, Kalaari and Blume and peaking at about $285M. Monthly actives fell from 9.4M in mid-2022 to about 3.1M by April 2023 as political interest faded and ads never paid for the servers. After buyout talks with Dailyhunt and others collapsed, it shut down in July 2024.

name: Hike
one_liner: Indian messaging app (Hike Messenger) that pivoted to the Rush real-money casual-gaming app
story: Kavin Bharti Mittal's Hike became a unicorn in 2016 ($175M Series D at $1.4B from Tencent, Foxconn, Tiger and SoftBank) as India's answer to WhatsApp, but WhatsApp won the market and Hike shut its messenger in January 2021. It pivoted to Rush, a real-money ludo and carrom app that drew 10M+ users and reportedly $500M+ gross revenue. India's 2025 ban on real-money online games cut its runway from seven months to four and Hike shut down entirely in September 2025.

name: Stoa School
one_liner: Online alternative-MBA program for working professionals
story: Stoa offered a cohort-based online alternative to the MBA for Indian professionals during the post-pandemic upskilling boom. It shut down in November 2024 without disclosing specific reasons, one of about a dozen funded Indian startups Inc42 counted as closing that year.

name: Urban Company
one_liner: Marketplace for trained, standardised at-home services from salon to repairs
story: Launched as UrbanClap in 2014, it trained and certified its own service pros (beauticians, cleaners, electricians) instead of running a loose lead-gen listing, the model that killed Homejoy in the US. It became a unicorn in 2021 at about $2.1B and listed in September 2025 with a Rs 1,900 crore IPO (about $220M at 86.5 INR/USD) that was ~104x subscribed; shares jumped ~58-62% on debut to a market cap near Rs 23,955 crore (~$2.77B).

name: Zomato (Eternal)
one_liner: Restaurant discovery site turned India's largest food delivery app

rounds.lead: Info Edge, Vy Capital, Sequoia Capital

story: Started in 2008 as Foodiebay, a site of scanned restaurant menus backed early by Info Edge, it pivoted into food delivery in 2015 and fought Swiggy to a duopoly after rivals like TinyOwl and Foodpanda India collapsed. Its July 2021 Rs 9,375 crore IPO (~$1.27B at 73.9) was ~38x subscribed and the stock closed day one up ~66% at a market cap of about Rs 98,700 crore (~$13.4B). It bought Blinkit in 2022 and renamed itself Eternal in 2025.

name: Swiggy
one_liner: Food delivery app with its own rider fleet, later adding Instamart quick commerce
story: Swiggy launched in Bengaluru in 2014 with its own delivery fleet, so restaurants without riders could deliver, and it raised over $3.5B from Naspers/Prosus, SoftBank and Invesco to reach a $10.7B private valuation in 2022. Its November 2024 Rs 11,327 crore IPO (~$1.35B) was one of India's largest that year, and the stock rose on debut to a market cap of about $12.3B. It remains loss-making as it spends heavily on Instamart to fight Blinkit and Zepto.

name: Blinkit (formerly Grofers)
one_liner: Grocery marketplace that pivoted to 10-minute delivery from dark stores
story: Grofers spent years as a slow, cash-burning grocery marketplace (valued at just $300M in 2018) before rebranding as Blinkit in late 2021 and pivoting to 10-minute delivery from dark stores. Zomato, already a ~9% holder, bought it in an all-stock deal for Rs 4,447 crore (~$568M) in 2022, below its $1B 2021 valuation because Zomato's own shares had fallen. Under Zomato, quick commerce became the group's main growth engine.

name: Zepto
one_liner: 10-minute grocery and essentials delivery from a dense network of dark stores
story: Founded in 2021 by teenage Stanford dropouts Aadit Palicha and Kaivalya Vohra, Zepto bet on 10-minute delivery from dark stores in dense Indian cities just as Gorillas, Getir and JOKR were retreating from the US and Europe. It reached a $7B private valuation and SEBI approved its IPO on 8 May 2026, but the listing was postponed and it raised over Rs 1,000 crore in a pre-IPO placement instead (per August 2026 reports).

name: Groww
one_liner: Mobile-first investing app for mutual funds and stocks aimed at first-time Indian investors
story: Four ex-Flipkart employees started Groww in 2016 to sell mutual funds to first-time investors, then added stocks and rode India's post-2020 retail-investing boom to become the country's largest broker by active clients. It moved its domicile from the US back to India before listing in November 2025 (IPO about Rs 6,632 crore, ~$767M at 86.5 INR/USD); the stock closed ~29% above issue on day one for a market cap of about Rs 795 billion (~$9B).

name: Lenskart
one_liner: Vertically integrated eyewear brand selling online and through thousands of own stores
story: Peyush Bansal started Lenskart online in 2010 but won by building its own lens manufacturing and a large chain of stores, turning a fragmented optician market into a branded D2C business. It listed on 10 November 2025 via a Rs 7,278 crore IPO (~$841M) that valued it at about Rs 69,700 crore (~$8.1B) at the issue price; the stock swung sharply on debut and closed roughly flat.

name: PhysicsWallah
one_liner: Low-priced online and offline test-prep coaching grown from a YouTube physics channel
story: Alakh Pandey's free YouTube physics lessons became a company in 2020 that sold exam-prep courses for a fraction of Byju's prices, and it was profitable enough to raise little capital (a $100M Series A in 2022 made it a unicorn). While Byju's and Unacademy imploded after the pandemic boom, PhysicsWallah listed in November 2025 with a Rs 3,480 crore IPO (~$402M) and jumped ~33% on debut, touching a market cap of about $5B.

name: Meesho
one_liner: Zero-commission value e-commerce marketplace that began as a WhatsApp reseller app
story: Meesho started in 2015 as an app for housewives and small resellers to sell products over WhatsApp, then dropped reselling and seller commissions to become a low-price marketplace for smaller-town shoppers. Unlike social-commerce peers such as DealShare that shrank after 2022, it cut burn hard and listed in December 2025 with a Rs 5,421 crore IPO (~$627M); shares jumped about 46% on debut.

name: Pine Labs
one_liner: Merchant payments company built on point-of-sale terminals and checkout EMI financing
story: Pine Labs began in 1998 as a fuel-card loyalty business and became India's leading POS-terminal network, adding brand-funded EMI at checkout. It listed in November 2025 via a Rs 3,900 crore IPO (~$451M) at a ~9.5% premium (listing price Rs 242), giving a debut market cap of about Rs 27,788 crore (~$3.2B), well below the ~$5B private valuation it was reported at in 2021; by July 2026 the stock traded about 40% below its debut level.

name: Paytm (One97 Communications)
one_liner: Mobile wallet and QR-code payments super app for Indian consumers and merchants
story: Vijay Shekhar Sharma's Paytm wallet exploded after India's 2016 demonetisation and blanketed merchants with QR codes, reaching a $16B private valuation in 2019 backed by Alibaba/Ant, SoftBank and Berkshire Hathaway. Its November 2021 Rs 18,300 crore IPO (~$2.48B at 73.9), then India's largest, fell about 27% on debut to a market cap near Rs 1.01 lakh crore (~$13.7B), and the RBI's January 2024 curbs on Paytm Payments Bank hit it again.

name: Nykaa (FSN E-Commerce)
one_liner: Inventory-led online beauty and personal-care retailer with its own brands and stores
story: Former banker Falguni Nayar launched Nykaa in 2012 to sell authentic beauty products online by holding inventory, avoiding the counterfeit problem of open marketplaces, and it was profitable before listing. Its November 2021 Rs 5,352 crore IPO (~$724M at 73.9) listed ~79% above issue and closed day one at a market cap of about Rs 1.04 lakh crore (~$14B), making Nayar India's richest self-made woman.

name: Policybazaar (PB Fintech)
one_liner: Online marketplace for comparing and buying insurance, plus Paisabazaar for loans
story: Yashish Dahiya, Alok Bansal and Avaneesh Nirjar started Policybazaar in 2008 to let Indians compare insurance prices online, pairing the site with large call centres because buyers still wanted advice. PB Fintech listed in November 2021 with a Rs 5,625 crore IPO (~$761M at 73.9), opening about 17% above its Rs 980 issue price, and later turned profitable.

name: Delhivery
one_liner: Tech-led express parcel and supply-chain network built for Indian e-commerce
story: Delhivery began in 2011 delivering restaurant food in Gurugram, then pivoted to parcel logistics for e-commerce sellers and built one of India's largest express networks with SoftBank's 2019 backing. It listed in May 2022 in a weak market with a Rs 5,235 crore IPO (~$666M at 78.6) priced at Rs 487 and closed day one roughly 10% higher.

name: Ola Electric
one_liner: Electric scooter maker selling direct to consumers from a mega-factory in Tamil Nadu
story: Spun out of Ola by Bhavish Aggarwal, Ola Electric built a huge scooter factory and sold online to ride India's EV subsidy wave, briefly becoming the country's top e-two-wheeler seller. Its August 2024 Rs 6,145 crore IPO (~$734M at 83.7) listed flat at Rs 76 and hit the upper circuit for a market cap of about Rs 40,200 crore (~$4.8B). It then stumbled on service complaints, regulatory notices and lost market share to TVS, Bajaj and Ather, and the stock fell far below its issue price.

name: Awfis Space Solutions
one_liner: Flexible workspace operator using landlord revenue-share partnerships to grow capital-light
story: Amit Ramani's Awfis built Indian coworking largely through managed-aggregation deals in which landlords fund fit-outs and share revenue, rather than WeWork-style long leases it paid for itself. While WeWork filed for US bankruptcy in 2023, Awfis listed in May 2024 with a Rs 599 crore IPO (~$72M at 83.7) at Rs 383 and opened about 13% higher.

name: Honasa Consumer (Mamaearth)
one_liner: House of online-first personal-care brands that started with toxin-free baby products
story: Varun and Ghazal Alagh launched Mamaearth in 2016 selling toxin-free baby products online, then used influencer marketing to spin up a portfolio of D2C brands and became a unicorn in 2022. It listed in November 2023 with a Rs 1,701 crore IPO (~$206M at 82.6) at a valuation of about Rs 10,400 crore, far below the ~$3B once floated, and opened only ~2% above issue.

name: Ather Energy
one_liner: Premium connected electric scooter maker with its own fast-charging grid
story: IIT Madras graduates Tarun Mehta and Swapnil Jain founded Ather in 2013 and spent years engineering a premium connected scooter and charging grid, backed by Hero MotoCorp. It listed in May 2025 with a Rs 2,981 crore IPO (~$345M at 86.5) priced at Rs 321, the first Indian EV-maker listing after Ola Electric, and gained share as Ola's service problems mounted.

name: Nazara Technologies
one_liner: Diversified mobile gaming, esports and kids-learning games group
story: Nitish Mittersain started Nazara in 2000 making mobile games for feature-phone carriers, then bought into esports (Nodwin) and kids' learning (Kiddopia) rather than betting on real-money gaming. Backed by Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, it became India's first listed gaming company in March 2021 with a Rs 583 crore IPO (~$79M at 73.9) at Rs 1,101 and listed roughly 80% higher.

name: ofo
one_liner: Dockless yellow bike-sharing app unlocked by smartphone, started on Peking University campus
story: ofo raised more than $2.2B in eight rounds from 2015-2018 (Alibaba, Didi, DST) and flooded Chinese and foreign cities with millions of cheap bikes in a subsidy war with Mobike. Bikes were vandalised and lost, rides were nearly free, and a takeover by investor Didi was resisted by the founder; by 2018-19 a Tianjin court found it had basically no assets while roughly 12 million users queued for deposit refunds worth about $170M. Seed/Series C figures from Pandaily; C post-money is the reported $370M pre-money plus $130M.

name: Bluegogo
one_liner: China's third-largest dockless bike-sharing service
story: Bluegogo put about 700,000 bikes on Chinese streets and planned a Seattle launch, but burned through roughly 600M yuan (~$119M at 2017 rates) and ceased operations in November 2017, the first major casualty of the bike-sharing bubble. Users struggled to recover deposits; Green Bike-Transit took over operations and Didi absorbed some assets and staff. Reported funding differs ($90M per TechCrunch, $58M per Bloomberg).

name: Wukong Bicycle
one_liner: Small Chongqing dockless bike-sharing startup with 1,200 bikes
story: Wukong launched about 1,200 bikes in hilly Chongqing with only mechanical locks and no GPS tracking. Within about five months roughly 90% of the bikes had disappeared, presumed stolen, and it shut down in June 2017, widely called the first failure of China's bike-sharing boom; the founder reportedly lost over 1M yuan.

name: Mobike
one_liner: Dockless smart-lock bike-sharing app with GPS-connected orange bikes

rounds.lead: Hillhouse Capital, Warburg Pincus, Sequoia China

story: Mobike built GPS-tracked smart-lock bikes and fought ofo city by city, raising five rounds in three years led by Tencent. Bleeding cash in the subsidy war, it was sold in April 2018 to Tencent-backed Meituan Dianping for a reported $2.7B equity value plus about RMB4.5B ($700M) of assumed debt, a deal brokered by Tencent's Pony Ma; Meituan later folded it into Meituan Bike.

name: Hellobike (Hello Inc.)
one_liner: Ant-backed bike-sharing and mobility app that started in smaller Chinese cities
story: Hellobike survived the bike-sharing war that killed ofo and Bluegogo by backing from Ant Financial, which co-led a $582M round in December 2018 reportedly valuing it at $2.3B, and by expanding into e-bikes and carpooling. It filed for a US IPO in April 2021 but withdrew in July 2021 after Beijing tightened overseas listing rules, and remains private.

name: Zilingo
one_liner: Fashion marketplace that pivoted into B2B supply-chain software and sourcing for Asian apparel makers

rounds.lead: Burda Principal Investments, Sequoia Capital India
Burda Principal Investments, Sofina, Sequoia Capital India

story: Zilingo started as a consumer fashion marketplace and pivoted to B2B software and sourcing for apparel makers, raising a $226M Series D in 2019 at a reported ~$970M valuation. In 2022 a fundraise surfaced questions about its accounting, CEO Ankiti Bose was suspended and then fired, a management buyout failed, and the company went into liquidation under creditors Varde and Indies Capital.

name: eFishery
one_liner: IoT fish feeders plus feed supply, financing and fish trading for Indonesian aquaculture farmers
story: eFishery sold automatic fish feeders and built feed, financing and fish-trading businesses for farmers, raising a $200M Series D in 2023 and reaching a reported $1.4B valuation. A whistleblower-triggered probe in late 2024 estimated management had inflated revenue by almost $600M in the nine months to September 2024 (about $752M reported vs about $157M actual), with two sets of books reportedly kept since 2018. In early 2025 it cut about 90% of staff while backers weighed liquidation, and an FTI report said investors might recover up to 10 cents on the dollar.

name: Investree
one_liner: Peer-to-peer lending marketplace funding working-capital and invoice loans for Indonesian SMEs
story: Investree matched lenders with Indonesian SMEs needing working-capital and invoice loans, and in October 2023 announced a ~$231M (EUR 220M) Series D anchored by Qatar's JTA International Holdings, structured through a joint venture. Regulator OJK revoked its licence on 21 October 2024 after it failed to meet the Rp 7.5B minimum-equity requirement and ignored warnings to inject capital and fix governance, sending it into liquidation. OJK then pursued ex-CEO Adrian Gunadi over alleged misuse of funds, and he was reportedly placed on Interpol's wanted list.

name: TaniHub
one_liner: Marketplace buying produce from smallholder farmers and supplying businesses, with a sister farmer-lending platform (TaniFund)
story: TaniHub bought produce directly from Indonesian farmers to sell to businesses and households, and ran TaniFund to lend to farmers. After the business wound down, prosecutors alleged irregularities and breaches of investment rules in about $25M of funding channelled into TaniHub and TaniFund between 2019 and 2023, and in 2025 arrested former CEO Ivan Arie Setiawan, a former board member and a former MDI Ventures CEO. Exact shutdown year and total funding are not confirmed by the sources collected.

name: Zenius Education
one_liner: Online video lessons and exam prep for Indonesian school students
story: Zenius was one of Indonesia's oldest online-learning brands for school students and scaled during the pandemic edtech boom. As the funding winter hit, it went through layoffs and in January 2024 said it would temporarily shut down operations, as reported in e27's roundup of the least-funded month of 2023. Funding totals are not confirmed by the sources collected.

name: Ula
one_liner: B2B wholesale app supplying stock and credit to small Indonesian mom-and-pop retailers
story: Ula supplied inventory to small warung shops through a B2B ordering app, one of several heavily funded Indonesian bets on digitising traditional retail. In 2023 it announced a temporary suspension of its business and then gradually shut down operations as the region's funding drought left thin-margin wholesale models unable to raise more. Funding totals are not confirmed by the sources collected.

name: Xinja
one_liner: App-only Australian challenger bank that won a full banking licence then handed it back
story: Xinja built an app-only neobank and won a full Australian banking licence, attracting 37,884 customers with more than A$252M in deposits. A promised A$433M investment from Dubai-based World Investments was paused, and with COVID-19 hitting capital markets it could not raise enough to keep operating. In December 2020 it returned 99.97% of deposits (the rest moved to NAB) and APRA revoked its licence.

name: Volt Bank
one_liner: Australian digital-only bank that shut after failing to raise a A$200M Series F
story: Volt was an Australian digital-only bank that raised almost A$85M in 2021 (about US$64M at 0.75) and went back to market in early 2022 for a A$200M Series F. When that raise failed, the board closed the business in June 2022 and handed back its banking licence, with about A$113M of deposits from some 6,000 customers returned or moved to NAB.

name: JOKR (Daki)
one_liner: 15-minute grocery delivery from dark stores; after exiting five markets it survives only as Daki in Brazil
story: Ralf Wenzel's JOKR launched in 2021 promising 15-minute grocery delivery from dark stores in New York and Latin America, merged with Brazil's Daki and became a unicorn with a $260M round at a $1.2B valuation in December 2021 (after a R$870M / $170M first round). As funding dried up it pulled out of the US (June 2022), Santiago and Medellin (November 2022) and Mexico (February 2023), then raised about $50M in 2023 at an $800M valuation to focus only on Brazil. Daki kept operating and later reports describe it as breakeven, with iFood taking a minority stake; total_raised counts only the reported rounds.

name: Merqueo
one_liner: Online supermarket delivering groceries from its own dark stores in Colombia, Mexico and Brazil
story: Merqueo built a Bogotá online supermarket with its own warehouses and expanded to Mexico and Brazil while talking up a US IPO. It closed Mexico in June 2022, entered Colombian business reorganisation in May 2023 with about COP 25.2bn (~$5.8M at 2023 rates) of pending obligations, and in July 2025 shut its stores and switched off its app after failing to secure new financing. Total raised is CB Insights' estimate; it also had a reported $22M IDB financing for Brazil.

name: Jüsto
one_liner: Mexico's store-less digital supermarket delivering groceries from its own warehouses
story: Ricardo Weder's Jüsto sold groceries online in Mexico with no physical stores, raising a $152M Series B led by General Atlantic in 2022 that El Financiero billed as minting a new Mexican unicorn, and expanding to Peru. After a $70M equity-plus-debt raise in October 2024 it wound down Peru, then announced it would stop operating in Mexico on 15 December 2025, citing financial, operating and strategic factors and struggling to make the model profitable. Weeks later, in January 2026, OMNi took over the brand and relaunched it, so the original venture ended in a rescue rather than an exit.

name: 123milhas
one_liner: Online travel agency selling cheap tickets built on airline miles and prepaid flexible-date promo trips
story: 123milhas sold discounted air tickets sourced from frequent-flyer miles, then pushed 'Promo123' flexible-date tickets and packages paid upfront for future travel, effectively betting that fares would fall without any hedge. When fares stayed high it suspended the Promo line in August 2023 and on 29 August filed for judicial recovery in Belo Horizonte, declaring R$2.308bn (~$462M at 2023 rates) of debt owed to around 700,000 creditors, most of them customers. Peer Maxmilhas also filed for judicial recovery as the Brazilian online travel sector's prepaid model unravelled.

name: Frubana
one_liner: B2B app supplying fresh produce and groceries to restaurants and small shops in Colombia, Mexico and Brazil
story: Frubana let restaurants and corner shops order produce and groceries wholesale through an app, cutting out middlemen, and expanded from Colombia to Mexico and Brazil. After layoffs in 2022, it announced in February 2024 that it would close Colombia and Mexico to concentrate on Brazil, then shut its last active market there, joining Merqueo among Colombia's high-profile startup closures. Analyses citing CB Insights grouped it with Jüsto as a LatAm example of the post-2022 funding crunch.
